4.text:
ABSTRACT
Diabetes is a widespread chronic disease that often remains undetected until serious
complications appear, so early risk prediction is important. This project presents a Smart
Disease Prediction System that predicts diabetes risk using supervised machine learning
classification on the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset (768 patient records, 8 clinical features).
The data was preprocessed in Python using pandas and NumPy by treating 652 biologically
impossible zero values as missing and imputing them with column medians, and the six most
informative features were selected using a combined ANOVA F-test and Random Forest
importance score. Four algorithms (Support Vector Machine, k-Nearest Neighbors, Random
Forest and Gradient Boosting) were tuned with GridSearchCV in scikit-learn and combined
into Soft-Voting and Stacking ensembles. All models were evaluated on a stratified 20% test set
using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score and ROC-AUC. The Soft-Voting Ensemble
achieved the best ROC-AUC of 0.818 with 74.0% accuracy, while Random Forest reached the
highest accuracy of 74.7%. SHAP explanations identified Glucose, BMI and Age as the
strongest risk factors. The final model is deployed in a Streamlit web application that provides
real-time predictions, a risk gauge, model comparison and plain-language reasons for each
prediction, demonstrating a practical and explainable decision-support tool for early diabetes
screening.
Keywords: Machine Learning, Diabetes Prediction, Classification, Ensemble Learning,
Voting Classifier, Stacking, Feature Selection, SHAP, Explainable AI, Streamlit

8.text:
CHAPTER 1
INTRODUCTION
1.1 Introduction
Diabetes mellitus is a chronic disease in which the body cannot properly regulate blood
glucose, either because it does not produce enough insulin or because it cannot use insulin
effectively. According to the World Health Organization, diabetes is one of the leading causes
of blindness, kidney failure, heart attacks and stroke. Many people live with diabetes for years
without knowing it, because early stages often show no clear symptoms. Early identification of
people at high risk allows lifestyle changes and medical treatment that can delay or prevent
serious complications.
Hospitals and clinics routinely record simple health measurements such as plasma glucose,
body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, insulin level and age. Machine learning (ML) can learn
patterns from historical records of these measurements and estimate the risk that a new patient
has diabetes. Unlike fixed rule-based cut-offs, an ML model can combine many measurements
at once and capture non-linear relationships between them.
This project, the Smart Disease Prediction System with Model Ensemble, uses the Pima
Indians Diabetes dataset of 768 patient records to build a diabetes risk predictor. Four
classifiers (Support Vector Machine, k-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest and Gradient
Boosting) are tuned and combined into Soft-Voting and Stacking ensembles. The best
ensemble is deployed in a Streamlit web application that shows the prediction, a risk probability
gauge, a comparison of all models, and the top three reasons behind each prediction using
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations).
1.2 Problem Statement
Diagnosing diabetes normally requires laboratory tests and a doctor's review, which may not be
available for regular screening in every location. Simple threshold rules (for example, glucose
above 126 mg/dL) look at one value at a time and ignore how several risk factors combine. On
the other hand, a single machine learning model can be unstable: different algorithms give
different answers for the same patient, and most models act as a "black box" that gives a yes/no
answer without any reason.
There is therefore a need for a system that (a) cleans real clinical data with missing and invalid
values, (b) combines several algorithms to produce a more reliable prediction, (c) explains each
1

9.text:
prediction in plain language so that users can understand and verify it, and (d) is easy to use
without programming knowledge. This project addresses these needs.
1.3 Objectives of the Project
• To collect the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset and preprocess it by treating biologically
impossible zero values as missing and imputing them with the median.
• To perform exploratory data analysis (class distribution, correlation heatmap,
histograms and box plots) to understand the data.
• To select the most relevant features using a combined score from the ANOVA F-test
and Random Forest feature importance.
• To implement and tune four classification algorithms (SVM, kNN, Random Forest and
Gradient Boosting) using GridSearchCV with 5-fold cross-validation.
• To combine the tuned models into Soft-Voting and Stacking ensembles and select the
best model by ROC-AUC.
• To evaluate all models using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC and
cross-validation accuracy.
• To explain individual predictions with SHAP and identify the most influential risk
factors.
• To deploy the best model in an interactive Streamlit web application for real-time
prediction.
1.4 Scope of the Project
In scope: binary prediction of diabetes (Diabetic / Not Diabetic) for adult female patients,
matching the population of the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset; data cleaning, exploratory
analysis, feature selection, training and comparison of six models, SHAP explanations, and a
locally run web application.
Out of scope: clinical diagnosis, prediction for male patients or children, integration with
hospital record systems, live data streams, and deployment on a public server. The system is an
educational decision-support tool and is not a replacement for medical advice.
2

10.text:
CHAPTER 2
SYSTEM OVERVIEW
2.1 Existing System
In the traditional approach, diabetes is detected through laboratory tests such as fasting plasma
glucose, the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) and HbA1c. A doctor compares each result
with fixed clinical thresholds and decides whether the patient is diabetic, pre-diabetic or
normal. Screening for risk before symptoms appear is usually based on simple checklists of risk
factors such as age, weight and family history.
Earlier computer-based approaches typically trained a single model, such as Logistic
Regression or a Decision Tree, directly on the raw dataset and reported only its accuracy.
2.2 Limitations of Existing System
• Laboratory testing requires clinic visits and costs, so it is not practical for frequent
screening of large populations.
• Fixed thresholds consider one measurement at a time and miss the combined effect of
several moderate risk factors.
• Raw datasets contain invalid zero values (for example, BMI = 0 or Blood Pressure = 0)
that mislead models when left uncorrected.
• A single model's errors are not balanced by any other model, so predictions can be
unstable.
• Models give no reasons for their predictions, so doctors and patients cannot verify or
trust them.
• Results are usually seen only as code output, not in an application a non-programmer
can use.
2.3 Proposed System
The proposed system is a complete machine learning pipeline with five Python modules.
data_prep.py downloads the dataset, replaces invalid zeros with column medians, generates
exploratory charts and selects the top 6 features. train.py tunes SVM, kNN, Random Forest
and Gradient Boosting with GridSearchCV, builds Soft-Voting and Stacking ensembles,
evaluates all six models and saves the best one. explain.py produces global feature-importance
3

11.text:
and SHAP charts and explains each individual prediction. app.py is a Streamlit web application
for real-time prediction, and predict.py is a command-line prediction tool.
The system overcomes the limitations above as follows: median imputation fixes invalid values
without deleting records; feature selection removes weak inputs; ensembles combine four
different algorithms for more stable predictions; SHAP gives the top three reasons for every
prediction; and the web application makes the system usable through simple sliders.
2.4 Software Requirements
• Operating System: Windows 10/11, Linux or macOS
• Programming Language: Python 3.9 or above (tested with Python 3.12)
• Libraries: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, SHAP, Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly, Streamlit,
joblib, requests
• IDE: Visual Studio Code / Jupyter Notebook
• Web Browser: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox or Microsoft Edge
• Data Format: CSV (comma-separated values)
2.5 Hardware Requirements
• Processor: Intel Core i3 / AMD Ryzen 3 or higher (Core i5 recommended)
• RAM: 4 GB minimum (8 GB recommended)
• Storage: 500 MB free space for the project, models and reports
• System Type: 64-bit operating system
• Internet: Needed once, to install libraries and download the dataset
4

SYSTEM IMPLEMENTATION
3.1 Overview of Development Tools
3.1.1 Development Environment: Python and Visual Studio Code
The project is written in Python because of its rich ecosystem of data science and machine
learning libraries. Visual Studio Code is used as the editor, and all scripts are run from the
terminal. The project is organised as separate Python modules (rather than a single notebook) so
that each stage, such as preprocessing, training, explanation and the web app, can be run and
tested independently. Figure 3.1 shows the project folder structure and setup commands.
Fig. 3.1 Development environment setup and project folder structure
3.1.2 ML Library / Framework: scikit-learn, SHAP and Streamlit
All libraries are installed with a single command, pip install -r requirements.txt. scikit-learn
provides the classifiers, GridSearchCV, ensembles, feature selection and evaluation metrics.
SHAP provides the explanation of predictions. pandas and NumPy handle the data, Matplotlib
and Seaborn draw the analysis charts, Plotly draws the interactive gauge and bar charts in the
app, Streamlit builds the web interface, and joblib saves and loads the trained models. Figure
3.2 shows the library versions with which the project was run and verified.

def load_and_preprocess_data():
download_data()
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH, header=None, names=COLUMNS)
# Impute biologically invalid zero values with column median
for col in ZERO_AS_MISSING:
df[col] = df[col].replace(0, np.nan)
df[col] = df[col].fillna(df[col].median())

CHAPTER 4
SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
The system follows a sequential machine learning pipeline, from raw data to an interactive web
application. Figure 4.1 shows the end-to-end architecture; each stage is described below.
Fig. 4.1 System architecture of the Smart Disease Prediction System
1. Data Collection: the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset (768 records, 8 features +
Outcome) is downloaded from its public source and cached locally as data/diabetes.csv.
2. Data Preprocessing: zero values in Glucose, BloodPressure, SkinThickness, Insulin
and BMI are converted to missing values and filled with the column median.
3. Exploratory Data Analysis: class distribution, correlation heatmap, histograms and
box plots are generated to understand the data.
9

17.text:
4. Feature Selection: each feature is scored with the ANOVA F-test and Random Forest
importance; the 6 features with the highest combined score are kept.
5. Train-Test Split: the data is split 80/20 with stratification (614 training and 154 test
records).
6. Model Training: SVM, kNN, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting are tuned with
GridSearchCV (5-fold cross-validation, ROC-AUC scoring).
7. Ensemble Learning: the four tuned models are combined into a Soft-Voting Ensemble
and a Stacking Ensemble with a Logistic Regression meta-learner.
8. Model Evaluation: all six models are compared on the test set using Accuracy,
Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC and 5-fold CV accuracy.
9. Best Model: the ensemble with the higher ROC-AUC (the Voting Ensemble, 0.818) is
saved as best_model.pkl.
10.Results and Insights: the Streamlit app uses the best model for real-time prediction,
and SHAP explains each prediction with its top three reasons.
10

18.text:
CHAPTER 5
DATA PREPROCESSING
5.1 Introduction
Real clinical data is rarely clean. The quality of a machine learning model depends directly on
the quality of its input data, so preprocessing is a critical step. In this project, preprocessing is
implemented in data_prep.py using pandas for data handling, NumPy for numerical
operations, scikit-learn for feature selection and splitting, and Matplotlib/Seaborn for
visualization.
5.2 Handling Missing Values
The dataset has no blank cells (isnull().sum() returns 0 for every column), but missing
measurements are recorded as 0. A value of zero is impossible for glucose, blood pressure, skin
thickness, insulin or BMI in a living person, so these zeros are treated as missing values. Figure
5.1 shows how many records are affected in each column.
Fig. 5.1 Invalid zero values (missing data) per feature before imputation
11

Table 5.1: Missing values and imputation values
Median used for

Glucose 5 0.7% 117.0
BloodPressure 35 4.6% 72.0
SkinThickness 227 29.6% 29.0
Insulin 374 48.7% 125.0

Each zero is replaced with NaN and then filled with the median of the column. The median is
preferred over the mean because these features are skewed (for example, Insulin has a long right
tail), and the median is not pulled by extreme values. Imputation keeps all 768 records instead
of deleting nearly half of them.
5.3 Data Cleaning
The dataset was checked for duplicate rows using df.duplicated().sum(), which returned 0, so
no rows were removed. Column names were added because the raw CSV file has no header
row. After imputation, no invalid zeros remain in the five medical measurement columns.
Pregnancies can validly be zero and is left unchanged.
Fig. 5.2 Class distribution of the target variable (Outcome)
Figure 5.2 shows that the classes are imbalanced (65.1% Not Diabetic, 34.9% Diabetic). This is
handled by stratified splitting (Section 5.7) and by using ROC-AUC, Precision, Recall and F1-
score in addition to accuracy.
12

20.text:
5.4 Outlier Detection and Range Validation
Outliers were inspected with box plots (Figure 5.3) and the interquartile range (IQR) rule,
where a value is an outlier if it lies below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. After
imputation, the main outlier counts were Insulin (346, many caused by values differing from
the imputed median), SkinThickness (87), DiabetesPedigreeFunction (29), BloodPressure (14),
Age (9), BMI (8) and Pregnancies (4).
Fig. 5.3 Box plots of all features after imputation (outlier check)
All remaining values lie within medically possible ranges (Table 3.1), for example Glucose 44–
199 mg/dL and BMI 18.2–67.1 kg/m². Because these values are plausible for real patients,
outliers were kept rather than removed. The tree-based models used are robust to outliers, and
SVM and kNN use standard scaling.
5.5 Feature Engineering / Encoding
All features are numerical, so no categorical encoding (one-hot or label encoding) is needed.
Feature scaling with StandardScaler (mean 0, standard deviation 1) is applied inside the SVM
and kNN pipelines, because both algorithms depend on distances between data points. Random
Forest and Gradient Boosting do not need scaling.
Feature selection reduces the 8 features to the 6 most useful. Each feature is scored by two
methods: the ANOVA F-test (f_classif), which measures how well a feature separates the two
classes linearly, and Random Forest Gini importance, which captures non-linear usefulness.
Both scores are normalised to the 0–1 range and averaged. Table 5.2 and Figure 5.4 show the
result.

The cleaned dataset with the 6 selected features is split into 80% training (614 records) and
20% testing (154 records) using train_test_split with stratify = Outcome and random_state
= 42. Stratification keeps the same 65:35 class ratio in both sets (the test set has 100 non-

used for hyperparameter tuning and for measuring model stability.
5.8 Summary
Preprocessing turned the raw data into a clean, reliable dataset: 652 invalid zero values across
five columns were replaced with medians without losing any records, outliers were checked
and found to be medically plausible, scaling was applied where needed, and feature selection
reduced the inputs to the 6 most informative features (Glucose, BMI, Age,
DiabetesPedigreeFunction, Pregnancies and Insulin). The stratified split ensures fair evaluation

CHAPTER 6
METHODOLOGY AND ALGORITHMS
6.1 Introduction
This project is a supervised binary classification problem: given a patient's health
measurements, predict whether the patient is Diabetic (1) or Not Diabetic (0). Four individual
classification algorithms from different families are used: a margin-based method (SVM), an
instance-based method (kNN), and two tree-based ensemble methods (Random Forest and
Gradient Boosting). These are then combined using two ensemble learning techniques, Soft
Voting and Stacking. SHAP is used to explain the predictions.
6.2 Classification Techniques
6.2.1 Support Vector Machine (SVM)
Working: SVM finds the boundary (hyperplane) that separates the two classes with the widest
possible margin. With the RBF (radial basis function) kernel, it maps the data into a higher-
dimensional space where a curved boundary in the original space becomes a straight one. The C
parameter controls the trade-off between a wide margin and correctly classifying training
points.
Advantages: Works well with a small number of features, handles non-linear boundaries
through kernels, and is less prone to overfitting with a suitable C value.
Application in Project: Used inside a pipeline with StandardScaler and probability=True so
that it can output risk probabilities for the ensembles. Tuned C ∈ {0.5, 1, 5} and gamma ∈
{scale, auto}; the best setting was C = 0.5, gamma = scale with the RBF kernel.
6.2.2 k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
Working: kNN stores all training records. To classify a new patient, it finds the k training
patients with the most similar measurements (smallest distance) and predicts the majority class
among them. The predicted probability is the share of neighbours that are diabetic.
Advantages: Simple and intuitive, needs no training phase, and naturally captures local
patterns in the data.
18

26.text:
Application in Project: Used with StandardScaler so that all features contribute equally to the
distance. Tuned k ∈ {3, 5, 7, 9} and weights ∈ {uniform, distance}; the best setting was k = 9
with uniform weights. kNN achieved the highest recall (0.593) of all models.
6.2.3 Random Forest
Working: Random Forest builds many decision trees, each trained on a random bootstrap
sample of the data and a random subset of features at each split. Each tree votes, and the forest
predicts the class with the most votes (or the average probability).
Advantages: Robust to outliers and noise, reduces the overfitting of single decision trees,
needs no feature scaling, and gives feature importance scores.
Application in Project: Tuned n_estimators ∈ {50, 100} and max_depth ∈ {None, 5, 10}; the
best setting was 50 trees with max depth 5. Random Forest is also used for feature importance
(Figure 6.2) and as the model explained by SHAP.
6.2.4 Gradient Boosting
Working: Gradient Boosting builds shallow decision trees one after another. Each new tree is
trained to correct the errors (residuals) of the trees built so far, and the learning rate controls
how much each tree contributes to the final prediction.
Advantages: Often gives high accuracy on tabular data, captures complex interactions between
features, and can be controlled through learning rate and tree depth to avoid overfitting.
Application in Project: Tuned n_estimators ∈ {50, 100}, learning_rate ∈ {0.05, 0.1} and
max_depth ∈ {3, 5}; the best setting was 50 trees, learning rate 0.05 and max depth 3.
6.3 Ensemble Techniques
6.3.1 Soft-Voting Ensemble
Working: Each of the four tuned models predicts the probability that the patient is diabetic.
The Soft-Voting Ensemble averages these four probabilities and predicts Diabetic if the
average is 50% or more.
Advantages: Balances the errors of individual models, gives more stable predictions, and uses
the confidence of each model rather than only its final vote.
19

27.text:
Application in Project: Built with VotingClassifier(voting="soft") on the four tuned models.
It achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.818) and was selected as the best model, saved as
best_model.pkl.
6.3.2 Stacking Ensemble
Working: Stacking trains a second-level model (meta-learner) on the predictions of the base
models. The base models' predictions are generated with 5-fold cross-validation so that the
meta-learner learns from predictions on data the base models have not seen. Here, Logistic
Regression learns how much weight to give each base model.
Advantages: Learns the best way to combine models instead of a simple average, and can give
more weight to the more reliable models.
Application in Project: Built with StackingClassifier using the four tuned models and
LogisticRegression as the final estimator (cv = 5). It achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.817, very close
to the Voting Ensemble.
6.4 Hyperparameter Tuning
Each base model was tuned with GridSearchCV, which tries every combination of the listed
parameter values using 5-fold cross-validation on the training set and keeps the combination
with the highest mean ROC-AUC. Table 6.1 lists the search space and the selected values.

6.5 Explainability with SHAP
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is based on Shapley values from game theory. It
measures how much each feature value pushed a particular prediction up or down compared
with the average prediction. A positive SHAP value increases the predicted diabetes risk, and a
negative value reduces it. In this project, SHAP's TreeExplainer is applied to the Random
Forest model.
Figure 6.2 shows the Random Forest's built-in (Gini) feature importance, and Figure 6.3 shows
the mean absolute SHAP value of each feature across the test set. Both agree that Glucose is by
far the most important feature, followed by BMI and Age.

6.6 Model Evaluation Metrics
Using TP (true positives: diabetic predicted as diabetic), TN (true negatives), FP (false
positives: non-diabetic predicted as diabetic) and FN (false negatives: diabetic patients missed),
the following metrics are used:
• Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN): overall correctness of predictions.
• Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the patients predicted Diabetic, the share who really are.
• Recall (Sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN): of the truly diabetic patients, the share the model
finds.
• F1-Score = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall): harmonic mean of precision
and recall.
• ROC-AUC: area under the ROC curve; measures how well the model ranks diabetic
patients above non-diabetic ones (1.0 = perfect, 0.5 = random guessing).
• 5-fold CV Accuracy: average accuracy across five splits of the training data, used to
check stability.

7.12 Key Findings
• Glucose is the most influential feature, confirmed by the ANOVA F-test (245.67),
Random Forest importance (0.263) and SHAP; BMI and Age come next.
• The Soft-Voting Ensemble generalised best by ROC-AUC (0.818), ranking risky
patients most reliably, and was selected as the final model.
• Random Forest had the highest accuracy (74.7%) and precision (0.683), while kNN
had the highest recall (0.593) and F1-score (0.615).
• Recall is the main weakness (0.50–0.59): about half of the diabetic patients in the test
set were predicted as Not Diabetic, which matters because a missed diabetic patient is
worse than a false alarm.
• Cross-validation accuracy (0.766–0.780) is close to test accuracy, showing that the
models are stable and not overfitting.

44.text:
CHAPTER 9
CONCLUSION
This project developed a Smart Disease Prediction System that predicts the risk of diabetes
from six routine health measurements. The Pima Indians Diabetes dataset was cleaned by
replacing 652 biologically impossible zero values with column medians, and the six most
informative features (Glucose, BMI, Age, DiabetesPedigreeFunction, Pregnancies and Insulin)
were selected using a combined ANOVA F-test and Random Forest importance score.
Four classifiers (SVM, kNN, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting) were tuned with
GridSearchCV and combined into Soft-Voting and Stacking ensembles. All six models were
evaluated on 154 unseen patients. The Soft-Voting Ensemble was selected as the best model
with a ROC-AUC of 0.818 and 74.0% accuracy, because averaging four different algorithms
gave the most reliable ranking of risky patients. Random Forest achieved the highest accuracy
(74.7%), and kNN the highest recall (59.3%).
SHAP explanations showed that high glucose is the strongest driver of diabetes risk, followed
by BMI and age, which agrees with medical knowledge. The Streamlit web application makes
the system practical: users move sliders and instantly see the prediction, risk score, each
model's opinion and the reasons behind the result. The project demonstrates the complete
machine learning workflow — data cleaning, analysis, feature selection, tuning, ensembling,
evaluation, explainability and deployment — applied to a real healthcare problem. Its main
limitation is moderate recall, which future work should improve before any clinical use.
37

45.text:
CHAPTER 10
FUTURE SCOPE
• Improve recall: lower the decision threshold below 50% or apply class balancing
(class weights or SMOTE) so that fewer diabetic patients are missed.
• Prevent data leakage: perform median imputation and feature selection inside a scikit-
learn Pipeline fitted only on training data.
• Explain the full ensemble: use SHAP KernelExplainer on the Voting Ensemble
instead of only the Random Forest model.
• Larger and more diverse data: train on datasets that include men, other age groups
and other populations so the model generalises better.
• Advanced models: try XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost and neural networks for higher
accuracy.
• Multi-disease prediction: extend the same framework to heart disease, chronic kidney
disease and liver disease.
• Cloud and mobile deployment: host the app online (for example on Streamlit
Community Cloud) and build a mobile version for wider access.
• Patient reports: fix and extend predict.py to generate downloadable PDF risk reports
directly from the web application.
